title: Getting the Latest Row: TOP 1 Needs an Index
description: Finding the latest row with TOP 1 + ORDER BY scans and sorts everything; an index on the sort column reads just the first row. Why it matters: "get the latest record" is an extremely common lookup, and this is exactly why it silently gets slower as history accumulates.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
This lesson tackles a pattern that trips people up because it *feels* like it should be cheap: fetching just the single most recent row with `TOP 1 ... ORDER BY SomeDate DESC`. Returning one row sounds fast — but if nothing keeps rows in date order, finding "the latest one" can mean reading the whole table.

Why does this happen? `TOP 1` only helps *after* the rows are already in the right order. If the table's only structure is organized by `OrderId` (not by date), then "the latest order" isn't sitting conveniently at one end — it could be scattered anywhere. To find it with certainty, SQL Server has to check every row's date, keep track of the maximum seen so far, and only after scanning everything can it say "this one wins."

Picture flipping through a stack of index cards filed by a random ID number, trying to find the one with the most recent date written on it. There's no shortcut — you have to look at every card's date, remembering the latest one you've seen, until you've checked them all. `TOP 1` doesn't save you any work if the cards aren't already sorted by date. The fix is an index sorted by that date column (descending): then "the latest row" is simply the very first card in the stack — no scanning required.

## Scenario
A dashboard shows the single most recent order: `SELECT TOP 1 ... FROM Orders ORDER BY OrderDate DESC`. On a 200,000-row table it is surprisingly slow for a query that returns just **one** row.

## Why it's slow
`Orders` is clustered on `OrderId`, but **nothing** orders the rows by `OrderDate`. To find the latest one, SQL Server must read *every* row (a **Clustered Index Scan**) and then perform a **Top-N Sort** to bring the newest to the top. Returning 1 row costs a full-table scan.

## What to look for
- A **Clustered Index Scan** on `Orders` reading ~200k rows.
- A **Sort** (Top-N) operator — the giveaway that the engine had to order the data itself.

## The concept
An index is stored **in order**. With an index keyed on `OrderDate`, the newest row is simply the last entry — SQL Server reads the tail of the index and stops. No scan, no sort. This is why an index on the `ORDER BY` column turns a full scan into a couple of reads.
hints: The query returns 1 row but is slow — look at how many rows the plan actually reads.
There is a Sort (Top-N) operator. SQL had to order the whole table because no index provides OrderDate order.
Create an index on the ORDER BY column: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_OrderDate ON Orders(OrderDate);
